nameStory: The spotted cucumber beetle gets its name from the distinctive black spots scattered across its bright yellow wing covers, like polka dots on a summer dress. While it's called a 'cucumber beetle,' this little troublemaker doesn't limit itself to cucumbers—it happily munches on corn, beans, squash, and many other garden favorites.
description: The spotted cucumber beetle is a small, oval-shaped beetle about the size of a ladybug, typically measuring around ¼ to ⅜ inch long. Its bright yellow-green wing covers are decorated with eleven black spots (though the count can vary slightly), making it quite distinctive among garden beetles. The head and legs are black, creating a sharp contrast with the colorful body. These active little beetles are common garden visitors throughout the warmer months.

idTips.label: Spotted wing covers
idTips.description: Bright yellow-green wing covers with black spots scattered across them—typically eleven spots, though some individuals may have slightly more or fewer

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small oval beetle about ¼ to ⅜ inch long, roughly the size of a ladybug but more elongated

idTips.label: Black head and legs
idTips.description: Shiny black head and legs that contrast sharply with the bright yellow body—the head looks almost helmet-like

idTips.label: Active behavior
idTips.description: Quick-moving beetles that readily fly when disturbed, making a soft buzzing sound as they take off

idTips.label: Plant association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near cucumber family plants (cucumbers, squash, melons) or corn, often feeding on flowers and leaves

habitat: You'll find spotted cucumber beetles in gardens, farms, and anywhere their favorite host plants grow throughout New England. They're especially common in vegetable gardens with cucumbers, squash, melons, or corn, but also turn up in flower gardens and along field edges. They prefer sunny, open areas and are rarely found in deep woods or shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late spring and begin seeking out young seedlings, especially cucumber family plants. This is when they cause the most damage to tender young plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults feeding heavily on flowers, leaves, and developing fruits. Multiple generations may overlap, so you'll see both fresh adults and worn individuals.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding into early fall, preparing for winter. Late-season adults often seek shelter under plant debris as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter, under bark, or in other protected spots. They're completely inactive and won't be seen until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called the 'eleven-spotted' cucumber beetle in some regions, these beetles are mathematical rebels—they can have anywhere from eight to fifteen spots, and some individuals even have their spots merged into stripes or irregular blotches!
confusionNotes: The spotted cucumber beetle is often confused with the striped cucumber beetle, which has three black stripes instead of spots. Remember: 'Spots or stripes?' If you see distinct black dots on yellow, it's the spotted version. The striped version looks like it's wearing a yellow shirt with black racing stripes.
contextualKnowledge: This beetle is also known as the 'southern corn rootworm' because its larvae feed on corn roots underground, while the adults prefer above-ground plant parts. The same species causes completely different types of damage at different life stages, which confused early agricultural scientists who thought they were dealing with separate pest problems.
compareHints: The spotted cucumber beetle is the only Diabrotica species commonly found in New England, but it's often confused with other small yellow beetles. Unlike the similarly-sized corn flea beetle, it doesn't jump when disturbed. It's also much smaller than most other yellow leaf beetles and has a more distinctly oval shape compared to the rounder ladybugs that might share its size.
